title: Germany invades Poland
subtitle: The invasion and the battle for time
author: R.G. Cruise
location: Poland and the Free City of Danzig
summary: Germany’s overwhelming advantages met effective resistance at bridges, fortified positions and village railway lines. The opening campaign turned on how quickly each army could move, recover and respond.
sourceMethod: The study compares German operational reporting with Polish military scholarship, museum accounts and contemporary diplomatic documents. Kennedy’s 1956 U.S. Army study is used for command assignments and identified operational reports, not its discredited cavalry-charge story or claims that Polish aviation was eliminated in the opening days. Reported advances describe leading units, not verified daily control boundaries. Disputed loss totals and Wieluń raid timings are qualified. Source notes identify the evidence and its limits.

sections.label: Mokra and the price of delay
The invasion becomes a European war

body:
At Tczew, the German invasion began with an attempt to keep something standing. The bridges over the Vistula were worth more to an advancing army intact than as wreckage in the river, and the Polish defenders had prepared to destroy them. Before dawn on 1 September 1939, German aircraft attacked the installations that would make demolition possible while a railway operation attempted to deliver troops to the crossings. The plan joined air power, surprise and transport in a single effort to save time. It failed. Warned of the approaching danger, Polish personnel frustrated the seizure, and the bridges were blown during the morning. Germany had begun its war with overwhelming advantages, but one of the first important results was a Polish success.

The attack on Tczew, usually placed at approximately 4:34 a.m., preceded the familiar bombardment of Westerplatte. It also introduces the central problem of the campaign more clearly than a photograph of a battleship can. German forces needed crossings, usable roads and opportunities to get behind Polish formations before those formations could withdraw. Polish commanders needed time to complete concentration, bring reserves forward and establish a defence that could survive the opening blows. A demolished bridge could interrupt that process for the attacker; a breakthrough elsewhere could make the interruption insufficient for the defender. The first day was fought through this unequal contest over time. [1] [2] The agreement signed in Moscow on 23 August had made the strategic setting more dangerous for Poland. Germany could attack without expecting Soviet intervention to preserve Polish independence, while the secret protocol anticipated territorial rearrangements at Poland’s expense. Yet the bargain was neither a completed partition nor a joint timetable for the operations of 1 September. The Red Army had not invaded. Polish government, armies and population still occupied a country whose defeat remained a military objective, not an accomplished fact. This study concentrates on the opening attack, then follows selected consequences through the Bzura fighting and Warsaw’s resistance. Those later developments are dated explicitly; the separate Soviet invasion is examined in the following study. [3]

The order and the pretext

By the time German troops crossed the frontier, the machinery of aggression had been running for months. The army’s plan, Fall Weiss, aimed to destroy Poland’s armed forces before they could escape the converging German offensives. The disputes over Danzig and transit across the Polish Corridor provided the diplomatic setting, but the operational design reached far beyond a border adjustment. The destruction of Czechoslovakia earlier in the year had enlarged Germany’s southern approaches into Poland, giving military planners another direction from which to threaten the Polish rear. Their task was to exploit that geography quickly enough to prevent an effective defence from taking shape. [4] There had already been a false start. Hitler intended the offensive to begin on 26 August, then postponed it after developments including the formal Anglo-Polish alliance signed on the 25th. A German commando detachment failed to receive the cancellation in time and attacked the railway route near the Jabłonków Pass. Polish resistance defeated the attempt to secure the tunnel and station for the coming army. The episode belongs to the transition between diplomacy and war, and it exposes the practical character of the preparations: the seizure of infrastructure was important enough to put small advance parties across the frontier before the main formations arrived. [5] On 31 August, Hitler issued Directive No. 1 for the Conduct of the War. It specified the next day and 4:45 a.m. for the attack, including the operation against the Tczew bridges. Its opening language blamed an allegedly intolerable situation on Germany’s eastern frontier, but the document itself recorded a decision for force made in advance. The same directive restrained German action in the west, where Hitler wanted Britain and France to bear responsibility for widening the conflict. He was ordering a war against Poland while trying to control how other powers would enter it. [6] The public explanation depended on a manufactured reversal of responsibility. SS personnel staged an incident at the Gleiwitz radio station on 31 August to suggest a Polish attack on German territory. Nazi press instructions then required the invasion to be presented as a defensive response and discouraged calling it a war. Across the frontier, the realities were unambiguous: German formations had received offensive orders, assembled for offensive tasks and crossed into Poland. The false border incidents supplied an excuse for a decision already taken; they did not cause the movement of the armies. [7]

Inside the diplomatic record

Proposals the ambassador never received

On the afternoon of 1 September, Polish ambassador Józef Lipski told the American chargé in Berlin that he had not even been furnished with the German proposals supposedly offered as a basis for negotiation. This was Lipski’s account, recorded by the American diplomat, and it undercuts the image of a straightforward settlement rejected after normal discussions. The army was already advancing while diplomats were still documenting how the appearance of negotiation had been maintained.

[8]

Two armies, two different problems

Germany’s advantage was considerable, although campaign totals can conceal the conditions under which particular engagements were fought. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives approximately 1.5 million German troops, around sixty divisions and more than two thousand tanks for the invading force. A Polish museum estimate places the forces Poland fielded during September at about 900,000. These are broad campaign measures, not synchronized headcounts of men in their battle positions at dawn on the first day. Polish mobilization and concentration remained incomplete. Germany could choose the places where its strongest forces would strike; Poland was still assembling parts of the army with which it had to resist them. [9] [10] The difference in organization mattered as much as the total number of soldiers. German armoured and motorized formations were concentrated for operational tasks, supported by artillery, engineers, communications and the Luftwaffe. Much of the German army remained ordinary infantry, and the speed of its leading formations exceeded that of the forces following them. That division of labour was useful. Tanks could force a passage or move around resistance while following infantry engaged bypassed Polish troops and secured routes. A German spearhead did not have to conquer every place behind it before threatening the next important junction. The offensive acquired its momentum from the interaction of these forces, rather than from the performance of tanks in isolation. [4] [11] Poland possessed trained infantry, artillery and anti-tank weapons capable of defeating German attacks. Its cavalry formations were equipped to fight on foot, using horses for movement, and their weapons included machine guns, anti-tank rifles and 37 mm guns. The problem was getting sufficient force to the right place, keeping neighbouring formations in contact and preserving the ability to move when a position became untenable. A gun that could destroy a tank did not give its crew the operational mobility of an armoured division. A regiment holding its ground could still lose its supply route or find an enemy force approaching from the rear. Polish competence at the point of contact and German superiority across the theatre could therefore coexist. [12] The air comparison was harsher. The RAF Museum sets roughly three hundred mostly obsolete Polish aircraft against more than thirteen hundred German fighters and bombers. Polish squadrons had dispersed to field airfields before the attack, so the familiar story that the Luftwaffe destroyed them on the ground at the outset is false. Their survival allowed real resistance, but dispersal could not cancel the disparity in numbers, performance and capacity to sustain operations. Germany could commit aircraft against the fighting front, transport system and targets farther inside Poland while the smaller Polish force faced difficult choices about where to expend its strength. [13] Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły’s armies also faced a geographical problem for which there was no painless answer. A shorter position deeper in the country would have surrendered important industrial districts, population centres and access to the sea before a serious battle. A defence near the frontier committed troops to a broad arc threatened from the west, East Prussia and the south. The Polish plan tried to defend essential territory while preserving the possibility of withdrawal and continued resistance. Its success depended on time, communications and assistance from abroad—the very conditions the German offensive was intended to disrupt. [4]

Reading the offensive

Two German army groups directed the attack. **Army Group North**, under Fedor von Bock, brought together Third Army in East Prussia and Fourth Army in Pomerania. Georg von Küchler’s Third Army faced the Polish northern approaches, including the fortified position at Mława on the route towards Warsaw. Günther von Kluge’s Fourth Army attacked across the Corridor, seeking to cut off Polish formations and establish land communications with East Prussia. Within Fourth Army, Heinz Guderian’s XIX Corps supplied a powerful mobile striking force. The northern operation thus combined a drive into Poland with the practical need to connect two German concentration areas separated by Polish territory. [4] **Army Group South**, commanded by Gerd von Rundstedt, contained the heavier concentration and three armies. Johannes Blaskowitz’s Eighth Army advanced towards Łódź and protected the northern flank of the principal thrust. Walther von Reichenau’s Tenth Army, with the strongest concentration of armour in the offensive, drove from Silesia towards the interior and Warsaw. Wilhelm List’s Fourteenth Army attacked through the southern approaches towards Kraków and farther east. Their movements were related: the forces on either side helped protect Tenth Army’s advance while threatening Polish formations that might otherwise turn against it. A reader following only the arrow towards Warsaw would miss much of the work required to keep that arrow moving. [4] The Polish commands were arranged around the territory they had to defend. Army Pomorze under Władysław Bortnowski covered the Corridor; Army Modlin under Emil Krukowicz-Przedrzymirski faced the threat from East Prussia. Farther west and south stood Tadeusz Kutrzeba’s Army Poznań, Juliusz Rómmel’s Army Łódź and Antoni Szylling’s Army Kraków. Army Karpaty covered the southeastern approaches, the Narew Operational Group the northeast, and Army Prusy formed the principal strategic reserve. Their names are useful geographical guides, but the spaces between these forces were as consequential as their individual positions. Germany’s converging advances threatened to separate them, close their withdrawal routes and commit the reserves before those reserves were fully assembled. [4]

Slovakia made the southern threat more extensive. Its German-dependent government permitted the use of Slovak territory and committed forces of its own. Two Slovak divisions took part from 1 September, attacking towards places including Bukowina Tatrzańska, Krynica and Muszyna. Their contribution was much smaller than Germany’s, but it widened the area Polish commanders had to watch and defend. The political destruction of Czechoslovakia had become an immediate military disadvantage for Poland: the southern frontier now offered an attacker opportunities that had not existed in the same form a year earlier. [14]

Crossings and strongpoints

The operation at Tczew demonstrates why the rivers on an atlas need to be read as military obstacles. Aircraft could fly over the Vistula; the vehicles and supply columns required a crossing. German bombing sought to interfere with the demolition system, while the railway approach attempted to deliver a force before the defenders could destroy the bridges. Polish railway workers at Szymankowo helped raise the alarm and frustrate the surprise. Enough of the defensive arrangements survived for the bridges to be demolished. The German operation had failed in its immediate purpose even though aircraft and troops had reached their objectives. [1] [2] Farther north, the battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on Westerplatte shortly before five in the morning. The Polish Military Transit Depot lay within the Free City of Danzig, and its defenders faced a concentration of firepower that appeared disproportionate to the small garrison. Major Henryk Sucharski commanded a force of a little over two hundred. The initial German assaults nevertheless failed, and the position remained in Polish hands at the end of the day. It would continue resisting until 7 September. Prepared defences and disciplined fire gave a small force an ability to survive that could not be inferred simply by counting men or comparing the size of their weapons. [15] [11] Mława presented a larger obstacle. Here the principal fortified position was defended by the Polish 20th Infantry Division within Army Modlin. Küchler’s Third Army encountered concrete defensive works, artillery and anti-tank fire after making progress earlier in the day. German infantry attacks met strong resistance; armour brought forward to break the position also failed to secure the expected result. The fighting continued on 2 September, while German forces sought opportunities to the east. The eventual threat to the defenders developed through outflanking and the deterioration of the wider position, rather than a simple repetition of the first frontal assault until Polish resistance disappeared. [16]

Mokra and the price of delay

At Mokra, northwest of Częstochowa, Colonel Julian Filipowicz’s Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade occupied ground between Army Łódź and Army Kraków. Its mission was to delay the enemy and maintain contact with neighbouring formations while the larger Polish deployment took shape. This was a professional assignment to a mobile covering force, and the terrain offered ways to carry it out. Woods restricted movement, the villages channelled approaches, and a railway embankment running along the eastern side of the position formed an obstacle to tanks. The brigade’s ability to use those features helped turn an apparent mismatch into a day of repeated German frustration. [17] The opposing 4th Panzer Division was a much stronger formation, with tanks, motorized infantry, artillery, engineers and supporting troops. Military historian Juliusz S. Tym gives its strength as 357 tanks; that is a divisional figure, not a claim that all those vehicles attacked the same Polish position simultaneously. The German advantage was therefore both substantial and more complicated than the image of a solid mass of tanks advancing against horsemen. Effective armour needed accompanying infantry and supporting fire. At several points the Polish defence exploited the vulnerability of tanks that had moved beyond adequate support, while German efforts became more coordinated as the day continued. [17] The Polish cavalry fought largely dismounted. Its anti-tank guns and artillery could engage the relatively lightly protected German vehicles, while the armoured train Śmiały added mobile firepower along the railway. Success required more than possessing the weapons: crews had to remain in action under bombardment, ammunition had to reach the guns, and threatened parts of the position needed support before they were overwhelmed. The terrain narrowed the choices available to attackers, allowing defenders to concentrate fire on approaches and openings. German assaults repeatedly entered dangerous ground without obtaining the decisive passage they needed. The brigade bought time through the use of weapons, terrain and local command. [12] It paid heavily for that time. Repeated attacks and bombardment wore down the defenders; positions had to be adjusted and units pulled back as pressure increased. The brigade’s subsequent withdrawal does not cancel what it accomplished on 1 September. Delaying forces are meant to interrupt an enemy’s timetable while retaining enough strength to continue fighting. Yet the reverse qualification is equally necessary: stopping a particular armoured division for a day did not restore the position of the whole Polish army. Other German formations could advance, and the defenders at Mokra still had to respond to developments outside the ground they had successfully contested. [17] [12]

Reading a battlefield total

A disabled tank is not always a destroyed tank

Published loss figures for Mokra vary, and a total of vehicles hit or temporarily disabled should not be presented as a count of permanent write-offs. Recovery and repair could return a tank to service. The securely established result is more useful here: the Polish brigade defeated repeated attempts at an immediate breakthrough. This account avoids turning disputed vehicle totals into an exact scoreboard.

[12] [17]
The related cavalry legend obscures a different engagement at Krojanty. There Polish cavalry charged German infantry, before coming under fire from armoured vehicles. The episode was transformed into the story of irrational horsemen attacking tanks with sabres, a convenient explanation that made Polish defeat appear to follow from national backwardness. The actual lessons of Mokra were harder for German propaganda to accommodate. Cavalrymen using modern anti-tank weapons could stop armour, and a supposedly irresistible formation could suffer a serious tactical check. Poland’s defeat requires an account of the larger military imbalance; a caricature of its soldiers explains very little. [10]

Measuring the advance

There is no honest single speed for the German advance on 1 September. Robert M. Kennedy’s U.S. Army reconstruction, drawing heavily on German operational records, reports that forward elements of Army Group South were three to four miles inside Poland by 6 a.m. and that some units had reached fifteen miles by late afternoon—roughly five to six kilometres and twenty-four kilometres respectively. These were advances by selected elements. They were not a uniform depth along the front, an army-wide daily average or proof that all the country behind the leading troops had been secured. The measurements describe how far particular parts of the offensive had progressed, alongside sectors where German attacks had been stopped. [11] A particularly instructive interruption came in the north on **2 September**. Kennedy records that armoured elements of XIX Corps temporarily outran their fuel and ammunition supply after the advance across the Brda. German supply columns had to fight through withdrawing Polish troops to reach the stalled tanks. This is a glimpse of vulnerability inside a successful offensive: the armoured point had moved faster than the system required to keep it fighting. Polish forces obtained only a temporary advantage, but the incident shows why a line drawn behind a spearhead cannot automatically be labelled secure territory. Enemy troops could remain between the tanks and their supplies. [11] By 3 September, the German Third and Fourth Armies had established contact across the Corridor, gravely worsening Army Pomorze’s position. In the south, the advance reached Kraków on 6 September, and the 4th Panzer Division reached Warsaw’s outskirts on the 8th. These milestones reveal a formidable capacity to exploit the opening battles, but arrival outside the capital did not mean possession of it. Warsaw continued to resist until 28 September. The contrast in dates measures the difference between a successful operational approach and the reduction of a defended city; it should not be collapsed into a claim that Poland had been defeated in a week. [11] [9] Army Poznań, comparatively little engaged at the outset, retained forces with which Kutrzeba could strike the exposed northern flank of the German Eighth Army. On **9 September**, his counteroffensive across the Bzura began around Łęczyca and Piątek; troops of Army Pomorze joined the fighting. Its initial success forced Germany to turn forces against a threat behind the advance towards Warsaw. The attack demonstrated that Polish commanders could identify and exploit an operational opportunity even after the frontier defence had broken down. [18] The opportunity narrowed as the surrounding situation changed. The retreat of Army Łódź undermined the prospect of a combined effort, while German redeployment threatened the Polish attackers with encirclement. Renewed fighting around Łowicz was followed by attempts to cross the Bzura and reach the Kampinos Forest. German forces concentrated against the crossing routes, and many Polish formations were destroyed or captured, although some troops reached Warsaw and Modlin. The battle’s significance lies in both results: it disrupted Germany’s timetable, yet the attacker possessed sufficient reserves and mobility to turn disruption into another encirclement. [18] Warsaw presented a different problem. German armour reached its outskirts on **8 September**, but early attempts to take the city failed. Urban defences deprived mobile formations of some of the freedom they had enjoyed on open roads, while retreating Polish units reinforced the capital. Its eventual capitulation on **28 September** followed a siege in which bombardment and damage to essential services made the position of civilians increasingly desperate. The three weeks between arrival and surrender were consequential: Germany could reach the capital quickly without being able to compel its immediate submission. Warsaw’s defence also maintained a visible centre of resistance while much of the field army was being forced into retreat or encirclement. [11] [9] “Blitzkrieg,” or lightning war, is therefore useful only with qualifications. The campaign displayed the effectiveness of concentrated armour, air power and converging movement; it also exposed failures in reconnaissance, combined action and supply. Kennedy’s reconstruction from German operational records documents these interruptions, while Juliusz S. Tym’s account of Mokra shows what unsupported tanks could encounter. Treating the victory as a flawless doctrine explains away the very fighting that determined how the advance unfolded. Germany’s superiority was sufficiently broad to absorb setbacks and recover the initiative more often than Poland could. [11] [17]

The war beyond the front

The destruction of transport and communications affected soldiers and civilians together. Air attack could delay reserves, interrupt a railway movement or make a road unsafe, while people fleeing the fighting entered the same transport network on which the army depended. To describe this only as interdiction would leave out the experience of those beneath the aircraft. At Wieluń, German bombing struck the town and its hospital on the first morning. An investigation by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance found that no Polish military units were present in the town on the eve of the invasion or on 1 September. The attack killed civilians, including hospital patients and personnel, far from any meaningful contest between equivalent military forces. [19] The exact timing of the first raid remains disputed, as does the complete number of victims. The investigation could document deaths but could not establish a final toll, and it challenged some higher figures repeated in commemorative accounts. The uncertainty over the clock and the count leaves the central findings intact: civilians were killed, patients and personnel died, and a hospital was struck in a town without the military units sometimes invoked to explain the raid. For the people beneath the bombs, the war arrived without the protection that even an inadequate defensive position might have offered. [19] [20] Violence also accompanied the ground forces. In the Parzymiechy area, close to the fighting south of Wieluń, Polish infantry resisted German troops through the first day before withdrawing towards Działoszyn. Paweł Żołądek’s research for the Institute of National Remembrance, based principally on witness testimony, describes German soldiers searching houses, seizing civilians and killing people during the occupation of the villages. Such actions belong inside the history of the advance. Treating the campaign only as a contest of arrows and formations can make civilians disappear at the very moment when the arrival of those formations transformed their lives. [21] German security forces also pursued political objectives behind the advancing armies. Einsatzgruppen—mobile security-police and Security Service formations—and other SS and police units participated in the destruction of potential Polish leadership. Arrests and killings of officials, clergy and educated professionals made conquest an attack on the institutions through which society might organize resistance. The occupation system examined in the October study would develop these policies further, but organized persecution was already part of the invasion’s consequences. [22] Military advantage and civilian vulnerability intersected throughout the day, but they were not the same kind of inequality. A Polish gun crew might have a chance to defeat the tank approaching it. A hospital patient or a family seized from a cellar possessed no comparable means of resistance. The invasion must be understood at both scales: the army attempting to defend the country, and people exposed to bombing, flight and deliberate violence. The speed of conquest is one part of that history. What the conquerors did when they arrived is another, equally necessary part.

The invasion becomes a European war

Britain and France had not declared war when the first day ended. Their governments demanded that Germany stop its attack and withdraw, while still testing whether diplomacy could prevent a wider conflict. The distinction mattered in Poland, where each interval of discussion was also an interval of German advance. The parliamentary record of 1 September shows the British government presenting withdrawal as the condition that could avert the consequences of its commitment to Poland. [23] Italy then proposed a conference involving the European powers. Reporting to Parliament on the evening of **2 September**, Chamberlain said that Britain could not take part while Poland remained under invasion and bombardment: German withdrawal would have to precede negotiations. The proposal therefore turned on a material question, not simply a willingness to talk. A conference held under continuing occupation might preserve Germany’s gains while postponing the moment when its opponents acted. Consultation with France also affected the timing of the British ultimatum. [24] On **3 September**, the British demand for an assurance of withdrawal expired at eleven in the morning. Chamberlain told the Commons that Britain was at war with Germany; France entered the war later that day. These were decisions for belligerency, with consequences extending far beyond a diplomatic protest. They nevertheless did not provide the immediate offensive relief on which Polish hopes depended. The French advance in the Saar was limited, while the British Expeditionary Force began arriving in France on **9 September**. The Allies were organizing for a sustained war, with defensive preparations and economic pressure playing central roles. Poland was fighting an emergency measured in days. [25] [9] [26] This discrepancy should be understood without pretending that a major Western offensive was a simple action requiring only an order. Mobilization, deployment and military assumptions constrained Allied choices. Those constraints do not change the result for Poland: the declarations internationalized the conflict but failed to divert enough German strength in time to prevent the destruction of its initial defensive position. Britain and France had accepted war with Germany; they had not found a way to make their intervention operate on the Polish campaign’s timescale. [26] The United States made a different set of decisions. Roosevelt proclaimed neutrality on **5 September**, imposing the duties of a non-belligerent state without requiring Americans to suppress their opinions or sympathies. On **21 September**, he asked Congress to repeal the arms-embargo provisions of the neutrality legislation. His proposal sought to change the rules governing trade with belligerents while keeping the United States out of the war; it was not an announcement of American military intervention, nor had the proposed repeal yet become law. American diplomacy, public sympathy and the supply question belonged to the international response, but none was equivalent to an army relieving Poland. [27] [28] Hungary’s conduct also resists a simple division between Germany’s friends and Poland’s friends. Its government pursued cooperation with Germany and had benefited from territorial revision, yet refused participation in the attack on Poland and denied the requested transit of German forces against it. It subsequently enabled Polish escape routes through Hungary towards the forces being assembled abroad. These decisions differed sharply from Slovakia’s participation in the invasion. Neighbouring governments operated under German pressure, but their responses were not identical, and those differences materially affected Polish opportunities for survival and continued resistance. [29] The first day had ended with Tczew’s bridges destroyed, Westerplatte still resisting and German attacks checked at Mława and Mokra, alongside dangerous penetrations elsewhere. Over the following days, Polish commanders struggled to connect such local successes into a defence that could endure. Germany could impose simultaneous problems faster than Poland could resolve them; Allied belligerency did not immediately reverse that imbalance. The Soviet invasion of **17 September**, examined in the [next study](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17), then attacked the remaining eastern space through which troops, officials and refugees were still trying to move.
